w: Glittertind rises 2,452 metres in Lom Municipality, making it Norway's second-highest peak after its near neighbour Galdhopiggen, just to the west. Both stand within Jotunheimen National Park, ringed by lesser-known summits - Trollsteineggje and Trollsteinrundhoe to the north, Grotbreahesten to the northeast - in one of the densest clusters of tall mountains in northern Europe.
s: Norway's second-highest peak, next door to its highest

w: Keilhaus topp stands 2,355 metres tall - high enough to rank among Norway's tallest mountains - yet it's often left off official lists because its topographic prominence is a mere 20 metres, barely separating it from neighbouring summits. It sits in Jotunheimen National Park between Galdhopiggen, Norway's true highest point, to the west and Store Styggehoe to the southeast.
s: A 2,355m peak too subtle to make the official list
_facts: Often excluded from official mountain rankings

w: At 2,469 metres, Galdhopiggen is the highest point in Norway, Scandinavia and all of Northern Europe. It rises in Lom Municipality within Jotunheimen National Park, encircled by a crowd of near-rivals - Keilhaus topp just to the east, Store Styggehoe to the southeast, Storjuvtinden and Skardstinden to the west - making this corner of Jotunheimen the highest ground on the continent's northern half.
s: Norway's, Scandinavia's and Northern Europe's highest point
_facts: Highest mountain in Norway, Scandinavia and Northern Europe
Located in Jotunheimen National Park, Lom Municipality

w: Kyrkja - Norwegian for 'the Church' - earned its name from a summit so steep it resembles a spire, and locals didn't believe it climbable until the 19th century. Today reaching the 2,032-metre top is a day's scramble up rock-covered slopes rather than a mountaineering feat. It used to hold snow year-round, but climate change has stripped much of that permanent cover from its flanks.
s: The peak too steep to climb until the 19th century
_facts: Name means 'The Church', for its spire-like shape
Not thought climbable until the 19th century

w: The Sjoa river threads from the famous lake Gjende through Ovre Sjodalsvatnet on its way down to the Gudbrandsdalen valley, passing the Maurvangen campground and Bessheim mountain lodge along its southwestern shore. The Sjoa is one of Norway's most popular rafting and kayaking rivers, and further downstream it carries paddlers past Ridderspranget - the 'Knight's Leap' - one of the valley's best-known landmarks.
s: A Jotunheimen lake on Norway's favourite rafting river
_facts: Lake on the river Sjoa, just outside the national park
Bessheim mountain lodge and Maurvangen campground nearby
Sjoa is a popular rafting and kayaking river

w: This shepherds' cabin in the Visdalen valley, 1,100 metres up between Norway's two highest mountains, first took in guests in 1836 and became a proper tourist station in 1881. It's now the largest lodge in Jotunheimen, with around 230 beds, reachable by car from March to October along one of the old paths that once crossed the range at 1,490 metres - higher than today's county road.
s: A shepherds' hut turned Jotunheimen's biggest lodge
_facts: Former mountain farm, guests first taken in 1836
Largest tourist cabin in Jotunheimen, ~230 beds
